galaxy.title: The Milky Way
galaxy.subtitle: Left-drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Right-drag (or two fingers) to pan
galaxy.disclaimer: This model illustrates shape and scale; it is not a dynamical simulation. Stars are scattered along logarithmic spirals with random noise, and the true positions of the spiral arms are still being remeasured — the map of the galaxy has been redrawn several times in the past two decades. The figures in the table come from observation.
galaxy.orbitBody: The Solar System does not travel on a fixed plane. As it circles the centre of the Milky Way, the gravity of the galactic disc pulls it back and forth through that disc, so its real path is a three-dimensional wave.
galaxy.orbitNotClosed: The ratio between the two periods is not a whole number, so the real orbit never closes: each lap returns the Sun to the same radius but a different point in its oscillation. The path drawn here rounds that to four oscillations per lap so it can close.

universe.scalesIntro: Each step below is tens to hundreds of times larger than the one before. The shell radii in the model are compressed to fit the view — drawn to true scale, the Milky Way would be smaller than a pixel.
universe.disclaimer: This model reproduces the morphology of the cosmic web — filaments, nodes and voids — rather than simulating it: no gravity between dark matter halos is computed. Node positions are random and correspond to no real galaxy cluster. The figures in the table come from observation.

universe.tourHint: To fly from Earth out to the cosmic web, see the Zoom journey.
universe.webIntro: On the largest scales the universe is not laid out at random. Hundreds of billions of galaxies gather along vast filaments of matter — the cosmic web — separated by enormous voids that hold almost no galaxies at all.

sky.searchPlaceholder: M31, Orion Nebula, Sgr A*, or coordinates…
sky.notFound: No matching object. Try a catalogue id, for example M31 or NGC 224.
sky.freeAimHint: The view is pointed at an arbitrary position on the sky, not at a catalogued object. Pick an object below to see its details.
sky.seeingBody: This is REAL observational data from the {survey} survey, not an artist's impression. The image is assembled from telescope filter channels, so colour and brightness are processed — they show what the instrument measured, not exactly what your eye would see at an eyepiece.
sky.oortLead: An icy shell wrapped around the whole Solar System, the source of long-period comets. This is a DIAGRAM, not a photograph: the Oort Cloud has never been observed directly. Its position is inferred from the orbits of long-period comets — Jan Oort proposed it in 1950 after noticing they all fall in from similar distances.
sky.oortScaleNote: LOGARITHMIC scale, not true proportion. Each ring is ten times the last. At true scale the orbits of all eight planets would be a single invisible dot at the centre — which is exactly what 100,000 AU means.
sky.oortInner: The Hills cloud, inner region — roughly 2,000 to 20,000 AU
sky.oortAu: AU stands for astronomical unit — roughly the mean Earth–Sun distance, about 149.6 million km. Light takes a little over eight minutes to cross it.
sky.oortOuter: The outer cloud — out to roughly 100,000 AU, about 1.5 light-years
sky.oortKuiper: The Kuiper Belt — 30 to 50 AU, where Pluto and Eris orbit
sky.oortUnknown: The boundaries drawn here are estimates, and uncertain ones, because no direct measurement exists.
sky.credit: Sky imagery by Aladin Lite and the HiPS surveys of CDS (Strasbourg Astronomical Data Centre). Coordinates from SIMBAD.

earthLive.title: Earth seen from point L1
earthLive.body: Full-disk images of Earth captured from the L1 Lagrange point by NASA's DSCOVR spacecraft.

earthLive.title: Earth from the L1 point
earthLive.metaDescription: Full-disk images of Earth from the EPIC camera aboard DSCOVR, taken at the L1 Lagrange point 1.5 million km away. NASA publishes them a few days after capture.
earthLive.intro: Every day a camera 1.5 million km away photographs Earth more than a dozen times. This is the most recent set NASA has released, replayed as one rotation. Processing and release take a few days, so the newest frame is usually two to four days old — the panel below gives the exact age of the one on screen.

spacecraft.detail: Launched in 2015, it sits at the L1 Lagrange point, where Earth's gravity and the Sun's balance out, so it holds its place on the line between the two using almost no fuel. Its main job is space-weather warning: it sees the solar wind about an hour before Earth does.

instrument.detail: It shoots through ten filters from the ultraviolet to the near infrared, one frame each. Three of them — red, green and blue — combine into the natural-colour image you see here. The other seven measure ozone, aerosols and cloud height.

cadence.detail: EPIC runs a full filter cycle every one to two hours, so each day brings more than a dozen sets. The data still has to reach the ground and be processed, so the newest image usually lags a few hours behind the shutter — close enough to call it today, not close enough to call it live.

earthLive.dayBody: Because DSCOVR always sits between Earth and the Sun. From there it can only see the lit half — not because the camera picks its moment, but because of the geometry of where it stands. That is also why the day–night terminator never appears in these images, unlike those from low-orbit satellites.
earthLive.colourBody: Almost. The image combines three filters at 680 nm (red), 551 nm (green) and 443 nm (blue) — the same part of the spectrum the eye uses, but as three narrow bands rather than the full continuous range. The result is close to what a person at L1 would see, a little heavier on atmospheric blue.
earthLive.limitTitle: What these images cannot tell you
earthLive.limitBody: One hemisphere only, and always the one facing the Sun at the moment of capture. Over a day Earth turns beneath the lens so the continents pass through in turn — but midnight is never visible. Following a specific spot on the ground needs a polar-orbiting satellite, not DSCOVR.

quick.orbitValue: Lagrange point L1, 1.5 million km away
quick.agencyValue: Operated by NOAA, camera built by NASA

earthLive.nextHint: Want to see where Earth sits among the things larger than it? The zoom journey runs from the observable universe down to here.
earthLive.credit: Images: NASA EPIC / DSCOVR, public domain. Data fetched from api.nasa.gov, with epic.gsfc.nasa.gov as a fallback.

detail.systemNote: System overview · structure identified from source anatomy

systemDescriptions.skeletal: Bones form the supporting framework of the body, protect organs, and provide attachment points for muscles. Their internal tissue also stores minerals and produces blood cells.
systemDescriptions.muscular: Skeletal muscles generate movement by pulling on their attachments. Together with tendons, they move joints, stabilize posture, and produce heat.
systemDescriptions.cardiac: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers. Its valves direct blood forward through the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
systemDescriptions.sensory: These structures contribute to special senses, including sight, hearing, and balance. Their specialized tissues detect stimuli and work with the nervous system to convey information.
systemDescriptions.arterial: The heart drives blood through the circulation. Arteries carry blood away from the heart to supply tissues or, in the pulmonary circuit, to the lungs.
systemDescriptions.venous: Veins return blood toward the heart. Superficial and deep networks collect blood from the tissues; the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back from the lungs.
systemDescriptions.nervous: The brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves carry and process signals. They support sensation, movement, coordination, and automatic regulation of body functions.
systemDescriptions.respiratory: The airways conduct air to the lungs, where oxygen and carbon dioxide move between air and blood. Breathing depends on pressure changes produced by respiratory muscles.
systemDescriptions.digestive: The digestive tract breaks down food, absorbs nutrients and water, and moves waste onward. Accessory organs contribute bile and digestive enzymes.
systemDescriptions.urinary: The kidneys filter blood and regulate fluid, electrolyte, and acid–base balance. Urine travels through the ureters to the bladder and exits through the urethra.
systemDescriptions.lymphatic: Lymphatic vessels return excess tissue fluid to the circulation. Lymph nodes and other lymphoid organs support immune surveillance and responses.
systemDescriptions.endocrine: Endocrine organs release hormones into the blood to coordinate processes such as metabolism, growth, stress responses, and reproduction.
systemDescriptions.reproductive: The male reproductive structures represented here contribute to sperm production, maturation, transport, and the production of sex hormones.
systemDescriptions.integumentary: The body surface provides an outer anatomical reference. The integumentary system forms a protective barrier and contributes to sensation and temperature regulation.
systemDescriptions.connective: Cartilage, ligaments, and other connective tissues support, connect, and separate structures. Their roles include stabilizing joints and distributing mechanical loads.

explanations.heart: A muscular pump in the chest. Its right side sends blood to the lungs; its left side sends blood through the systemic circulation.
explanations.liver: A large organ beneath the right side of the diaphragm. It processes absorbed nutrients, produces bile, and synthesizes many proteins carried in the blood.
explanations.brain: The central organ of the nervous system. Its interconnected regions support perception, movement, memory, language, and the regulation of bodily functions.
explanations.stomach: A muscular chamber between the esophagus and small intestine. It stores and mixes food with acid and enzymes before releasing it into the duodenum.
explanations.spleen: A lymphoid organ in the upper left abdomen. It filters blood, removes aging blood cells, and participates in immune responses.
explanations.pancreas: An abdominal organ with digestive and endocrine roles. It supplies enzymes to the small intestine and releases hormones including insulin and glucagon.
explanations.urinaryBladder: A muscular reservoir in the pelvis that stores urine arriving from the kidneys through the ureters.
explanations.trachea: The main airway connecting the larynx to the bronchi. Its cartilage supports keep the airway open during breathing.
explanations.diaphragm: A broad muscle separating the chest and abdomen. When it contracts, it increases chest volume and helps draw air into the lungs.

aboutSheet.title: Anatomy data source
aboutSheet.lead: Explore the adult male reference anatomy from BodyParts3D.
aboutSheet.scope: 2,234 individual meshes and 3,432 named concepts from an adult male reference anatomy.
aboutSheet.limits: This reference does not contain every human structure or variation. Named concepts can contain multiple pieces; each source mesh is rendered once.
aboutSheet.purpose: Colors and system groupings are designed for exploration. The geometry is simplified for the web, and short explanations provide general educational context. This is an anatomical reference, not a diagnostic or surgical tool.
aboutSheet.sourceText: BodyParts3D, © The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Sciencepedia did not create this dataset; the geometry was converted in axes and units, simplified, and repackaged for the browser.
aboutSheet.appText: The 3D viewer is adapted from Human Atlas by ashemag, released under the MIT License.
aboutSheet.translation: Vietnamese names are AI-assisted translations following anatomical nomenclature and have not been expert-reviewed; the original English name is always shown alongside.

page.heading: About the Human Body Atlas
page.intro: This atlas takes the BodyParts3D reference anatomy apart into 2,234 individually selectable pieces grouped into 15 systems. Orbit, zoom, toggle systems, search a structure by name, isolate it, or explode the whole body into its parts.
